prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought an optical frequency standard to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B061 as my single prize part and my preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1. After the chair's questions, the novelty objection is the one that matters, so let me answer it directly. Hall and Hansch gave us a way to count optical cycles, and Wineland and Haroche showed how to control and read out one quantum system. The lattice clock answers a different question: how do you keep an enormous number of neutral atoms, held still by light, from having their clock transition disturbed by that same light? Katori's magic wavelength is the answer, and it is an idea about the atom's structure, namely that the ground and excited states can be made to experience the same light shift. Without it, there is no trade between statistics and perturbation, and a neutral-atom clock cannot reach the 10^-18 level. That step is not a refinement of a comb or of an ion trap. Ye then showed, by identifying and measuring blackbody radiation, lattice light shifts, collisions and density effects one at a time, that the floor really is near 10^-18, and cross-comparisons between laboratories on several continents (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) show that the result is not one group's measurement. The consequences I care about are fundamental: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, limits on the drift of constants and on dark-matter couplings. The redefinition of the second follows from the result and should neither push the timing forward nor hold it back.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that a reader of the prize list could see 2005, 2012 and 2026 as three awards for precision laser spectroscopy. I think the magic-wavelength lattice distinguishes this one, but it is a judgement and Kroll's phrase that the discovery content is engineering physics rather than a new phenomenon is not frivolous. The second weakness is credit. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Bloom and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups all got clocks to this level, and Ye's comb work was in part already honoured in 2005. A two-name prize draws a line through a contested field, and I cannot verify the early lattice-clock chronology from the files; I am working from memory. Third, if the committee wants the discovery of new quantum matter rather than a controlled-quantum-system achievement, B013 answers that better than B061 does.

responses.point: Kroll calls the lattice clock an engineering-physics achievement rather than a new phenomenon, and asks whether a narrow citation for the invention and realisation of the lattice clock fully answers the 2005 and 2012 overlap objection.
responses.response: I agree that the citation must be narrow, and I have changed my wording to say the optical lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, not optical clocks in general. I disagree that this is only engineering. The magic wavelength is a statement that two atomic levels can be tuned to shift together under a trapping field, which is atomic structure, and it is what makes the 10^-18 level reachable for neutral atoms. Narrow wording does not remove the overlap with 2005 and 2012, but I think it answers it: those prizes did not cover this step. I would also rather not mention geodesy or the second in the citation, as you say, because that is the part that invites the objection.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether members who ranked B061 first would prefer it on maturity grounds, and how the pending SI redefinition of the second should affect timing.
responses.response: Yes, maturity is part of my reason, though not the whole of it. A claim at 10^-18 is checked every time two clocks are compared, and several laboratories in different countries have made those comparisons, so a wrong claim would already have been found. On the redefinition, I would give it no weight in either direction. If the decision were made next year, it would not change what Katori and Ye did, and if it is delayed, it does not make the physics less secure. I take your point that B008 is the more elegant idea, but I do not see it as more urgent, and as I said in round 1 the configuration is awkward with Bohm deceased.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B013 because a simple continuum model predicted flat bands and nature confirmed them, and says that the discovery does not depend on the unsettled pairing mechanism, while naming B061 as the safer fallback.
responses.response: I find the prediction and confirmation argument persuasive, and it is the kind of closure I would like to see. Where I differ is on how settled the central question is. You and Eriksson say the platform stands regardless of mechanism, and the reproduction across groups supports you on that. But I am a theorist who does not have the condensed-matter knowledge to judge sample dependence, and I notice that Mehlig, Eriksson, Olsson and you all list the unresolved pairing and the attribution to Cao and earlier band-structure work as open. That tells me it would be safer for the committee to wait a few years than to decide on the credit now. I could accept B013 if the attribution questions are answered from the record, and I have put it first among my alternatives for that reason.

responses.point: Olsson says she wants to be absolutely sure the credited people did the original work before settling on B013, and reads the mandate as favouring an experimentally verified discovery with an original experiment.
responses.response: I share your standard and would apply it to B061 as well. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and carried out the first demonstration, so the concept and the first experiment are clearly his. For the precision demonstration at the 10^-18 level, Ye's group is the clearest, but Lemonde, Lisdat and others contributed, and that is exactly the limit I accept. I read the mandate the same way as you, and I think B061 meets it, since this is an original experiment, not a development of an existing technology. To me the difference between our two positions is that for B061 the credit question is narrow and the two names are stable across all the opening ballots, whereas for B013 the first author and earlier theorists remain unresolved.

responses.point: Eriksson says that a prize for the moire platform rather than a settled mechanism could look premature next to the topological insulator and Cirac-Zoller cases, which have longer records, and that a second condensed-matter prize soon after 2016 may shift the committee toward B061.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and I am grateful for the point, because it is an argument that comes from a condensed-matter physicist rather than from my corner of the field. I would not rest my case on the proximity of prizes in other fields, since that should not decide a prize, but I do agree that B019 and B034 have longer records than twisted graphene. On the question of whether I could accept B013 as the 2026 prize: yes, on one condition, that the attribution of the 2018 experiments and the flat-band theory is checked against the record by someone who can check it, and that the committee accepts it is rewarding the platform and not the mechanism.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct step and not a third award in the 2005 and 2012 line; this is a judgement I cannot settle from the files.
Whether two names suffice given Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and Bloom, and how to treat Ye's earlier comb work; I rely on memory and have not seen the record.
Whether B013 attribution (Cao, Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell) is resolved by the record; I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on this.
Whether a multi-part prize combining B061 with B034 would be better, given that the three-person limit forces a drop of a name; I do not see a way to make it fit without weakening one part.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. My long-standing collaboration with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups does not concern B061, B013 or B034, and nothing in my profile links me to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Cirac or Zoller. Atomic many-body theory is my own field, so I judge B061 as an insider and would say that openly; I would flag it if attosecond or photoionization time-delay work reached the shortlist.
